name: Double eyelid surgery (Asian blepharoplasty)

card.summary: Surgery that creates an upper-lid crease; one of the most commonly performed cosmetic procedures in East Asia, with a large surgical literature but few controlled trials.
card.aka: Asian blepharoplasty, supratarsal fold creation, double eyelidplasty
card.note: Static folds, asymmetry and need for revision are discussed in the literature.

quick.overview:
Double eyelid surgery creates a supratarsal fold, the crease in the upper lid that many East Asian eyelids lack. Surgeons describe incisional and suture-based approaches, and the procedure is often combined with epicanthoplasty.

Wikipedia describes it as among the most popular procedures in many East Asian countries, particularly South Korea, with operations typically lasting 30 to 60 minutes. Published evidence is mainly surgical case series, including patient-reported outcome measures such as FACE-Q.
quick.mechanism: The crease forms when the skin is attached to deeper lid structures such as the levator aponeurosis. Techniques include external incisions with fixation to the orbicularis, septum or aponeurosis, and buried sutures without a skin incision.
quick.risks: Literature describes static, overly depressed folds, multiple folds, asymmetry and failed folds requiring revision, plus suture-related problems with buried-suture methods.

lead: Double eyelid surgery, also called Asian blepharoplasty or supratarsal fold creation, is an operation that forms a crease in the upper eyelid. Surgical authors note that Asian upper lids often have no superior palpebral fold, along with excess fat, pretarsal skin laxity and a medial epicanthal fold.[2]

Wikipedia describes it as among the most popular cosmetic procedures in many East Asian countries, particularly South Korea, with typical operations lasting 30 to 60 minutes and sutures removed after 5 to 7 days.[11] Authors in the plastic surgery literature say preferences for double eyelids have grown with cultural exchange.[2]

Methods fall broadly into incisional and suture (non-incisional) approaches. Evidence is mostly retrospective surgical series; a FACE-Q validation study measured patient satisfaction in 200 cases.[1][3][9]

paras: Authors describe the characteristic features of the Asian upper eyelid as lack of a superior palpebral fold, abundant fat, pretarsal skin laxity and a medial epicanthal fold, and report that many Asians regard double eyelids as attractive.[2] A review describes the anatomy of the Asian upper eyelid, patient assessment, an external incisional technique and pitfalls.[3]

Wikipedia distinguishes double eyelid surgery in younger patients, aimed at creating a fold, from Asian blepharoplasty in older patients, which can also remove surplus skin. It notes that the term blepharoplasty dates to 1818.[11]

The incisional method uses an upper lid incision with deeper fixation. Variants include orbicularis oculi to levator aponeurosis fixation,[6] and a technique using septoaponeurosis junctional thickening, reported in 680 patients, designed to produce a dynamic fold and avoid a static overdepressed one.[1] Buried-suture methods avoid a skin incision and are covered in the article on non-incisional double eyelid surgery.
Epicanthoplasty is often added; techniques including Y-V advancement and 'lazy S-curve' epicanthoplasty have been described.[2][4][8]

Reported problems include static folds,[1] multiple upper-lid folds requiring correction,[10] and failed folds requiring corrective revision, discussed in a 2004 paper on strategies after previously failed revisions.[7]
A retrospective study validated FACE-Q appearance satisfaction scales for minor-incision double-eyelid blepharoplasty in 200 young Asian patients.[9]

Wikipedia reports that many foreigners travel to South Korea for the procedure and cites cost estimates of roughly US$2,000 to $4,000, depending on technique and surgeon. Its references include scholarship on the 'Korean Look' and medical nationalism, indicating the topic is also studied as a cultural phenomenon.[11]

Human evidence is dominated by surgical case series and technique reports,[1][2][3][4][7][8][10] plus a FACE-Q validation study.[9] A registered, unrandomised study (NCT04001660, 30 participants) examined subbrow blepharoplasty combined with double eyelid surgery in Asian women.[12] No large randomised comparison of techniques was found.

timeline.event: The term 'blepharoplasty' is coined by von Graefe (per Wikipedia).[11]
Strategies for corrective surgery after failed Asian blepharoplasty published.[7]
Septoaponeurosis junctional thickening technique reported in 680 patients.[1]
FACE-Q scales validated for double-eyelid blepharoplasty in young Asians.[9]
